paper_title: Auto-Research Agent on MSA Organization to Improve Protein-Protein Complex Structure Prediction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Protein-complex structure prediction with AlphaFold 3 depends on MSA content, depth, and cross-chain pairing. Current pipelines apply uniform recipes, typically maximizing depth and pairing by species, yet even whether cross-chain pairing helps AF3 remains contested. We show that the value of both depth and pairing is strongly target-dependent, so no single recipe is optimal across interfaces. We introduce an autonomous agent that treats a frozen AF3 as a black-box experimental instrument. For each target, the agent formulates biological hypotheses, analyzes and reorganizes the MSA, and iteratively refines sequence selection and pairing using predictor label-free signals alone. On 1{,}015 protein--protein interfaces from three benchmarks released after AF3's training cutoff, the agent improves overall interface DockQ over AF3's default pipeline and fixed MSA recipes on every benchmark, while using on average 60\% fewer MSA sequences than the default. Gains are largest for inter-species heteromers, where species-based pairing is unreliable: mean DockQ increases from 0.465 to 0.612 on FoldBench and from 0.482 to 0.562 on HD439. The improvements arise from both sequence construction and pairing policy, including deliberate non-pairing. These results recast MSA design as a target-specific problem and show that an autonomous agent can adapt it at test time through biological reasoning and self-directed, confidence-guided experimentation.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Deep learning has transformed protein structure prediction. AlphaFold2 (AF2) (Jumper et al., 2021) achieves near-experimental accuracy for many proteins by exploiting co-evolutionary signals in multiple sequence alignments (MSAs): by aligning homologous sequences, MSAs reveal conserved positions and correlated substitutions that constrain residueresidue contacts. For complexes, the same principle extends across chains. AlphaFold-Multimer (Evans et al., 2021) and AlphaFold3 (AF3) (Abramson et al., 2024a;b) combine unpaired MSAs for each chain with paired MSAs, in which homologs of different chains are matched by species so that correlated substitutions across the interface inform inter-chain geometry; RoseTTAFold (Baek et al., 2021) relies on MSA features in similar way. Prediction accuracy therefore depends on MSA quality, which varies substantially across targets: sparse, redundant, or incomplete alignments can limit accuracy. One response is to bypass alignments altogether. MSA-free predictors such as ESMFold (Lin et al., 2023) and HelixFold-Single (Fang et al., 2023) instead encode evolutionary regularities in protein language models. Like MSA1 based methods, however, their accuracy decreases for targets with few homologs (Lin et al., 2023; Fang et al., 2023). For heteromeric complexes, recent benchmarking (Luo et al., 2026) challenges the assumption that precise cross-chain pairing is essential: on average, increasing the depth of unpaired alignments helps AF3 as much as or more than species-based pairing, trend that extends to antibodyantigen complexes. These findings, however, concern single construction axis, depth versus pairing, and are reported as aggregate trends; how this axis interacts with other construction choices, and whether such trends hold for individual targets, remains untested. This ambiguity calls for an agent that decides, for each target, how deep to search, what to filter, and how to pair sequences, and that refines these decisions using feedback from downstream structure prediction. Evaluator-guided LLM auto-research offers relevant precedent. In combinatorial optimization and algorithm design, FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), EoH (Liu et al., 2024), ReEvo (Ye et al., 2024), and AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) use LLMs to search over programs scored by an evaluator, discovering heuristics that outperform hand-designed ones. These successes rest on two conditions: instances are homogeneous, so one program serves the whole problem class; and the score is the objective itself (e.g., tour length or number of bins), so optimizing it solves the task. MSA construction satisfies neither: Target-dependent optima. Proteins differ widely in family size and diversity of available homologs, so strategy that works well for one target often fails to transfer to another. No ground-truth signal as guidance. For new target the true structure is unknown, and the only available feedback is AlphaFold3s confidence scores (e.g., pLDDT, ipTM) (Abramson et al., 2024a), which are the models own estimates of accuracy rather than measurements of it. Optimizing them directly risks exploiting their miscalibration, so they must be weighed against direct analysis of the MSA and predicted structure. The central challenge is therefore not to find single better heuristic, but to build general-purpose environment in which an agent can explore, reflect, and refine construction strategy for each new target. Our contributions are: Auto-Research Agent. We introduce an autonomous agentic framework that keeps the structure predictor in the loop. The agent iteratively proposes, evaluates, and refines targetspecific MSAs using only the predictors label-free feedback. SOTA Performance. Across three proteinprotein benchmarks, the agent consistently improves over AF3-Default setting and other heuristic strategies, while using substantially shallower MSAs, with average depth reduced by approximately 60%. Target-specific MSA reasoning. The agents key capability is to turn target-specific biological diagnoses into an iterative hypothesis-testing process, reading the predictors confidence feedback to refine its MSA construction step by step.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: MSA construction and pairing. Building an MSA for complex involves two decisions: how deep each chains alignment is, and how its rows are paired across chains. Retrieval tools such as JackHMMER (Eddy, 2011), HHblits (Remmert et al., 2012), and MMseqs2 (Steinegger & Söding, 2017), as used in ColabFold (Mirdita et al., 2022), determine each chains depth and diversity. Pairing methods then match rows across chains, using species and genomic proximity (Mirdita et al., 2022), coupling or mutual-information objectives (Bitbol et al., 2016; Bitbol, 2018), or differentiable matching (Lupo et al., 2024; 2025). Which decision matters more is contested: across hundreds of heterodimers, most reported pairing gains stem from the accompanying increase in depth (Luo et al., 2026). Portfolio-based pipelines hedge across these choices by generating alternative inputs for each target and keeping the best: DeepMSA2 (Zheng et al., 2024b) selects among MSAs from hierarchical database searches using AlphaFold-based scores; MULTICOM (Liu et al., 2023; 2025) builds alternative alignments, templates, and paired MSAs from multiple sources of evidence; and CAF3 (Neupane et al., 2026) evaluates pre-enumerated MSA and template variants for AF3. These pipelines adapt to each target only through selection: candidates are produced by fixed rules, and the scores do not inform which new candidates to generate. 2 Autonomous research agents. LLM agents increasingly conduct research in proposeevaluate revise loop. In domains with reliable evaluators, they evolve programs and heuristics against executable scores (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024) and automate machine-learning research whose experiments return measurable outcomes (Lu et al., 2024; Schmidgall et al., 2025). Because the evaluator is trustworthy, research reduces to optimizing against it. Agents in chemistry and biology, by contrast, have primarily served different role: orchestrating specialized domain tools to plan experiments, analyze intermediate results, or execute established research workflows (Bran et al., 2024; Ghafarollahi & Buehler, 2024; Shen et al., 2024; Xin et al., 2024; Sinclair et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2026) rather than iterate toward an objective. When they do iterate in silico, they score candidates with computational proxies such as predicted structure confidence (Swanson et al., 2025), implicitly treating these proxies as ground truth; trustworthy closed-loop feedback has so far required physical experiments (Boiko et al., 2023).

sections.title: 3 PRELIMINARY
sections.content: Proteins, Complexes, and MSAs. Proteins are chains of amino acids (20 common types); writing each as letter turns protein into string, its sequence. Many proteins function as complexes of several chains, which fall into three categories: homomers (identical chains), intra-species heteromers (distinct chains from one organism, e.g., hemoglobins α and β chains), and inter-species heteromers (chains from different organisms, e.g., viral protein bound to host receptor, or an antibody bound to an antigen). Homologs are proteins in different species that descend from common ancestral gene and share similar sequences and structures. multiple sequence alignment (MSA) aligns querys homologs so that corresponding positions share column. Because residues in spatial contact tend to mutate together, co-varying columns indicate structural proximity. singlechain MSA captures only intra-chain coevolution. paired MSA extends this signal across chains by matching each chains homologs by source species, so each row holds proteins from one organism. Pairing therefore mainly benefits intra-species heteromers, whose chains coevolve within one organism. MSA representation. Consider target complex with protein chains, and let xc ΣLc be the query sequence of chain c, where Σ is the amino-acid alphabet augmented with gap token; we omit from chain-level quantities when clear. Chain has an unpaired MSA Uc ΣN Lc, whose rows are homologs retrieved independently for that chain, and paired MSA Pc ΣN pLc. For each row index i, the corresponding rows across chains contain homologs associated with the same UniProt organism ID, with all-gap rows for chains lacking corresponding homolog. These rows define putative cross-chain correspondence. The complete MSA representation is = {(Uc, Pc)}C c=1. Let Hk denote the homologs retrieved for all chains of target k. target-specific MSA construction strategy gk pairs, orders, and combines these sequences into an MSA proposal Ak = gk(Hk). DockQ evaluation. We score each interface with DockQ (Basu & Wallner, 2016), which lies in [0, 1] and combines three measures of agreement with the reference structure: the fraction of native interface contacts recovered (Fnat), the RMSD of interface residues (iRMSD), and the RMSD of the smaller chain after superposing the larger one (LRMSD). An interface on complex target is pair of chains in contact in the reference structure. Given an MSA proposal Ak, AF3 generates structure samples with ranking scores {rs}S s=1. sections.title: 4.1 OVERVIEW
sections.content: We formulate the design of MSA representation as an autonomous agentic exploration process. The framework comprises three components: 1) the agent that iteratively proposes MSA representation; 2) the predictor such as AF3 that generates structure predictions from each proposal; and 3) the runtime environment that executes tool calls, enforces budgets, and manages the prediction-derived signals observed by the agent. Concretely, given multichain complex target k, the agent constructs an initial MSA representation proposal A(1) that includes unpaired MSAs for every chain and paired MSAs across chains (Preliminaries 3). The agent then enters an iterative refinement process. In each round r, it submits A(r) ) as observables. This feedback is derived exclusively from the outputs of and does not require access to the ground-truth structure (Appendix A). Based on this feedback, the agent may write and execute its own analysis programs before producing refined proposal, A(r+1) to and receives prediction-derived feedback signals F(A(r) . This proposalfeedback cycle continues until the submission budget is exhausted or the agent concludes further improvement is unlikely. Finally, the agent nominates one MSA representation from its previous proposals. We evaluate by submitting it to and comparing the resulting predicted structure with the ground-truth structure. We then get the evaluation signal E(A k) using DockQ, as defined in Preliminaries 3. It is worth noting that, in our main experiments, the runtime exposes only F(A(r) ) to the agent. It computes E(A(r) ) silently and never exposes these signals through the agents context or workspace. As an ablation study, we consider an oracle setting in which E(Ak) is visible to the agent, as described in Appendix F. sections.title: 4.2 AUTONOMOUS AGENT WITH PREDICTOR-IN-THE-LOOP
sections.content: Double-loop Architecture. Each run on target operates via hierarchical double-loop architecture across three nested levels  (Fig. 1)  ; 1) An outer-loop episode is sequence of proposal rounds that drives MSA representation evolution. It ends when the agent nominates one previously submitted proposal as the final proposal k; 2) inner-loop proposal round is an optimization loop consisting of two consecutive phases. In Construction phase, the agents iteratively analyzes the target and earlier findings until it successfully submit proposal A(r) to generator G. In Refleck tion phase, the agent interprets generator feedback F(A(r) ) and writes structured summary mr to reflect its learning. 3) An LLM turn is single model invocation, which may issue one or more actions. proposal round typically spans many turns (Appendix K.1). Round 1 is mandatory control that submits the default AF3 input, so the default is always nominable candidate and the reference for all later proposals. Actions. At turn of prospective round r, LLM is prompted to generate action ar,t together with the action-specific arguments ϕr,t. The available actions depend on the phase: Acon = {analysis, submit, finish}, Aref = {analysis, submit_round_summary}. (1) The Acon and Aref represent the available actions in Construction and Reflection phases, respectively. The action definitions are: analysis runs an agent-written Python program in the sandbox (Section 4.3) and returns its output. It does not change the phase; at most calls are allowed per reflection. submit executes builder script, validates the resulting proposal, runs G, and returns F(A(r) ), consuming one unit of budget. The agent is instructed to weigh proxy confidence, robustness across seeds, and biological plausibility. sections.title: 4.3 RUNTIME AND WORKSPACE
sections.content: The runtime separates what the agent sees from what it keeps: the LLM context is reset every round (Section 4.2), whereas an episode-scoped workspace persists. This section describes the workspace, the sandbox in which analysis code runs, and how the runtime validates actions and enforces budgets. Workspace. Each episode has private workspace. The runtime writes the target inputs into it at the start of the episode and adds predictor feedback after each valid submission, restricted to what the current execution profile makes visible. The agent adds its own files, such as analysis programs, derived statistics, notes, and candidate MSA organizations, through analysis. The runtime thus supplies the target and the predictor signal, while the agent decides how to process that signal and what to keep. Workspace files never enter the context automatically and must be read through analysis. The folder layout is given in Appendix 5 Analysis sandbox. Rather than fixed set of analysis tools, the agent receives general-purpose programming environment, so it can decide which evidence matters for given target and compute it itself. Each analysis call specifies an objective and Python program, which runs in fresh, isolated process. The process may read the target inputs, visible predictor feedback, and existing workspace files, and may write only to the agent-writable part of the current workspace. Network access is disabled to prevent ground-truth leakage. The process terminates after the call, and its textual output is appended to the context as or,t. Action validation. The runtime checks every action against its schema before execution, including proposal submissions and memory entries. failed check is returned as the tool output and followed by another LLM turn; it changes the context but not the proposal, the memory, or the predictor-call count. If turn contains no action, the runtime appends continuation instruction. Budgets and termination. Each episode has an LLM exploration budget and submission budget. Every LLM turn during exploration, including reflection and correction turns, counts toward the former; each successfully completed submission counts toward the latter. Once the LLM exploration budget is exhausted, analysis and new submissions are disabled. Up to two additional LLM turns are reserved for any pending round summary and finish; these turns are included in the reported LLM-call total. The episode is marked unsuccessful if the required finalization is not completed within the allowed calls.

sections.title: 5.1 BENCHMARK DATASETS
sections.content: We evaluate on three proteinprotein interface benchmarks comprising 1,015 interfaces in total, all released after AF3s training cutoff (details in Appendix B.2 and B.1). FB-v1-pp (278 interfaces; 194 homomeric, 84 heteromeric) is the protein-protein subset of the published FoldBench benchmark (Xu et al., 2026). It excludes interfaces similar to AF3s training data at the chain and whole-complex level, so that accuracy reflects what AF3 infers from the input MSA rather than what it has memorized. FB-v2-pp-hard (299 interfaces; 168 homomeric, 131 heteromeric) is hard subset of FoldBench-v2 currently under development. It retains only interfaces whose local binding geometry and residues differ substantially from AF3s training set. HD439 (438 heteromeric interfaces) is public benchmark (Luo et al., 2026) comprising entirely of heterodimers: 99 inter-species and 339 intra-species pairs.

sections.title: 5.2 AGENT SETUP
sections.content: Predictor. We use AlphaFold 3 (v3.0.2) as with the FoldBench inference protocol (Xu et al., 2026): 10 recycles and five diffusion samples for each of five fixed random seeds, shared across all targets and conditions, giving 25 structures per submission. Within each target, all conditions also use the same query sequences and templates, so differences in predicted structures arise from the MSA input alone. The default condition uses the MSAs and species-based pairing of AF3s standard data pipeline. Agent proposals instead specify each chains MSA row by row; homologs placed in the same row across chains form one row of the complex MSA, so the agent controls both which sequences are included and which are paired across chains (Appendix B.4). LLM Setting. The agent uses GLM-5.3 with temperature 0.2, maximum reasoning effort, and maximum response length of 32,768 tokens. Each target is processed in an independent episode whose first proposal is the AF3-Default control (Appendix B.5). Budget Setting. Each episode allows at most 60 completed generator runs, including the initial Default proposal, and 600 LLM calls in total. Failed or invalid submissions are not counted, and the agent may stop early by nominating final proposal k. The analysis Python program has execution time limit 120s (Appendix B.6).

sections.title: 5.3 MSA INPUT BASELINES
sections.content: We compare our agent with the following baselines: AF3-Default is the initial MSA proposal generated by AF3 Default pipeline. It is submitted directly to the predictor without iterative refinement or proposal selection. mMSA is the fixed MSA representation strategy where only monomeric alignments are provided, without additional cross-chain pairing. pMSA is the strategy in which the monomeric alignments are supplemented with cross-chain paired sequences. uMSA is the strategy in which the monomeric alignments are supplemented with unpaired UniProt hits. Controlled comparisons. The agent and AF3-Default always start from identical MSA resources, so Agent vs. AF3-Default is our primary comparison: it isolates the effect of iterative refinement and proposal selection. The three other baselines are controlled with respect to one another, but not always with respect to the agent. On the FoldBench sets, they are built from separate HHblits and UniProt searches. Because pMSA and uMSA draw on the same pool of hits, their difference isolates the effect of pairing, but their differences from the agent also reflect MSA source and construction. On HD439, the agent and all baselines use the MSAs released with the benchmark (Luo et al., 2026), whose unpaired, paired, and UniProt-enriched variants serve as mMSA, pMSA, and uMSA, so all comparisons there are input-matched. Implementation details are given in Appendix B.3.

sections.title: 6.1 MAIN RESULTS
sections.content: As Table 1 shows, the agents nominated MSA representations achieve the highest Qmean, average Qranking, and average Qoracle across all benchmarks. At the benchmark level, Qmean rises from 0.584 to 0.604 on FoldBench-v1-pp, from 0.556 to 0.583 on FoldBench-v2-pp-hard, and from 0.583 to 0.624 on HD439. In six out of the eight interface-type subsets across the three benchmarks, and its gains on Qmean over AF3-Default are statistically significant (Appendix Table 5). All methods are scored on the same 25 structures from five seeds; the agents additional predictor runs (6.01 per target on average) are used only for search, so the gains do not come from sampling more structures. Because nomination uses confidence on these same structures, we also re-predict the nominated MSAs with fresh seeds and find that the gains persist (Appendix D). Sequence construction and pairing policy. The agent controls both the sequences included for each chain and their pairing structure, including which sequences are intentionally left unpaired. To assess the contribution of this pairing policy, we independently shuffle the row order of each chain in the agents proposed MSA (Appendix Table 5). This preserves the per-chain sequence content but destroys the proposed pairing structure: selected pairs are broken, while intentionally unpaired sequences can be presented to AF3 as arbitrary pairs. The comparison therefore measures the value of the agents complete pairing policyboth pairing and deliberate non-pairingrather than pairing alone. For homomers and inter-species heteromers, where informative cross-chain pairing is not expected, shuffling does not significantly change Qmean, indicating that the gains primarily arise from sequence construction. For intra-species heteromers, however, shuffling significantly lowers Qmean, showing that the agents pairing policy provides additional benefit. On the 339 intra-species targets in HD439, preserving this policy accounts for approximately half of the gain over AF3-Default (0.014 out of 0.029), with the remainder attributable to sequence construction.

sections.content: The agents final result depends on two abilities: finding better MSA during exploration, and picking good one at the end. For each interface, let be the mean DockQ of AF3 Default, the highest mean DockQ among all proposals the agent tested, and the mean DockQ of the proposal it nominates. We call BD the exploration gain, the largest improvement the agent found, and BN the nomination regret, the part of that improvement lost when choosing. The final improvement is their difference: = (B D) (B ). (3) Figure 2 compares both quantities on 278 interfaces from 238 matched FBv1-pp targets under two settings: the main setting with predictor feedback, and an oracle setting with ground-truth feedback, in which the agent also sees DockQ during the search and its best tested proposal is nominated automatically. With predictor feedback, both steps limit the final result. Using DockQ Qmean as metric, the exploration gain exceeds 0.05 on 34 of the 278 interfaces, and the nomination regret exceeds 0.05 on 13 interfaces. On average, the best tested proposal is 0.035 above AF3 Default, but nomination gives back 41.0% of this gain, leaving final improvement of 0.020. With ground-truth feedback, the agent always nominates its best proposal (target-level), so the interface-level nomination regret is almost zero and the exploration gain equals the final gain. The exploration gain itself also rises from 0.035 to 0.059 (71.7%). more accurate feedback signal thus improves both steps: it helps the agent search more effectively and removes the loss at nomination. sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced an autonomous research agent that optimizes MSA representation for proteincomplex structure prediction at test time. Using frozen predictors confidence signals, the agent writes and executes analyses, accumulates evidence in memory, and adapts unpaired MSA depth and cross-chain pairing for each interface without ground-truth structures or gradients. Across FoldBench-v1, FoldBench-v2, and HD439, this approach improves overall average accuracy and confidence-based model selection, with smaller gains in best-case accuracy. The discovered strategies also provide insight into the target-dependent value of pairing and depth. Together, these findings establish adaptive MSA representation as an effective training-free approach and demonstrate how autonomous agents can use model feedback to investigate and improve inference in structural biology.

FoldBench-v1 is the proteinprotein subset of FoldBench (Xu et al., 2026). To limit overlap with AF3s training data, FoldBench includes only PDB entries deposited between 2023-01-13 (AF3s validation cutoff, later than its 2021-09-30 training cutoff) and 2024-11-01, and removes interfaces similar in sequence or structure to reconstructed AF3 training set. The subset contains 279 interfaces from 239 targets. We exclude 8bvk, whose single homomeric interface could not be processed because LLM API content filtering interrupted the agent, from all methods. The evaluation set thus contains 278 interfaces from 238 targets: 194 homomeric and 84 heteromeric (65 intra-species, 19 inter-species). FoldBench-v2. FoldBench-v2 is an extension of FoldBench currently under development. For each interface released after the AF3 training cutoff, its similarity to eligible pre-cutoff reference structures is estimated using interface sequence identity and structural mapping coverage, rather than global sequence similarity. For candidate reference, the score is the mean of the identity coverage products on the two sides of the interface; the interface similarity is the maximum score over eligible direct and swapped chain matches. This is proxy based on retrieved pre-cutoff references, not an exact measure of similarity to AF3s training set. The benchmark samples 100 interfaces from each 0.1-wide similarity bin over [0, 1]. We evaluate its hard subset, defined by the strict criterion < 0.3. One interface at the boundary (S = 0.300) is excluded, leaving 299 interfaces from 283 assemblies: 168 homomeric, 100 intra-species heteromeric, and 31 inter-species heteromeric interfaces. HD439. HD439 (Luo et al., 2026) contains 439 heterodimeric targets, each contributing one interface: 340 intra-species and 99 inter-species. We exclude 7acw, an intra-species target whose official MSA is unavailable, leaving 438 targets and 438 interfaces (339 intra-species and 99 interspecies). Based on PDB initial release records, the structures were released between 2021-10-06 and 2024-08-14, all after AF3s training cutoff of 2021-09-30. Dataset overlaps. At the PDB-entry level, our evaluated FoldBench-v1 and FoldBench-v2 sets share 15 entries, FoldBench-v1 and HD439 share 17 entries, and FoldBench-v2 and HD439 share 10 entries. Three entries are present in all three benchmarks. We retain overlapping entries in their respective benchmarks without special treatment. For each benchmark experiment, we independently run the agent on every target, including those shared with other benchmarks, and report results separately for each benchmark. B.3 MSA INPUT BASELINES Default. Paired and unpaired MSAs are generated using the AlphaFold 3 v3.0.2 data pipeline with UniRef90 (2022_05), MGnify (2022_05), UniProt (2021_04), and Small BFD 16 (bfd-first_non_consensus_sequences.fasta), and processed by AF3s built-in pairing procedure (Appendix B.4). This condition also serves as the agents initial proposal A(1) . Controlled baselines on FoldBench. The controlled baselines share monomeric alignment generated by HHblits against Uniclust30 (2018_08) with an E-value threshold of 103, minimum query coverage of 50%, maximum sequence identity of 90%, and two iterations. Additional hits are retrieved from UniProt (2021_04) using one JackHMMER iteration with reporting and inclusion Evalue thresholds of 104 max_sequences=50000. Both pMSA and uMSA use the same merged pool of raw search hits, without an additional global hit cap during baseline construction. mMSA: the monomeric alignment only. pMSA: the monomeric alignment supplemented with complete cross-chain pairs. Hits are grouped by exact header TaxID without taxonomic-rank normalization, retaining only TaxIDs represented in every protein entity. Within each group, hits are matched by their the jth hit of each entity forms one paired row, up to order in the merged alignment: the smallest group size across entities. Candidate rows are sorted by the product of their original per-entity row indices, with ties broken by the index sum, within-group rank, and TaxID. The first 8,191 non-query paired rows are retained, or all rows if fewer are available. uMSA: the monomeric alignment combined with the same UniProt hit pool used for pMSA, without pairing, and filtered using HHfilter at 99% sequence identity. Controlled baselines on HD439. We use the MSA files publicly released with the HD439 benchmark as fixed baseline inputs and do not regenerate them. The released conditions correspond to the authors monomer/unpaired, species-paired, and UniProt-enriched constructions, which we denote as mMSA, pMSA, and uMSA, respectively. In the released files, these conditions are stored under the unpaired, paired, and uniprot variants. According to the original paper, the underlying searches use HHblits against Uniclust30 (2018_08) and MMseqs2 against UniRef30 (2022_02) and the ColabFold environmental database (2021_08). The paper reports HHblits candidate settings spanning two iterations, E-values of 1040, 1010, 103, and 1, coverage thresholds of 50% and 75%, and identity thresholds of 90% and 100%, with up to 12 selected candidates. It does not provide complete command lines or all details of the AlphaFold2-based candidate-selection procedure; therefore, we treat the released MSAs as the authoritative baseline inputs rather than attempting an independent reconstruction. Source mismatch between agent and controlled baselines. On HD439, the agent, Default, and fixed MSA baselines all use the official precomputed MSA resources. The agent and Default use initial inputs constructed from comb_filter.a3m, with rows assigned to the paired or unpaired channel according to whether AF3 can parse species identifier. The uMSA baseline places the same combined alignment entirely in the unpaired channel; mMSA uses the supplied monomer alignments, and pMSA additionally uses the supplied paired alignments. On FBv1 and FBv2, the agent and Default share the same precomputed input MSAs, whereas the fixed baselines use separately constructed Uniclust30 and UniProt-based MSAs. The AgentDefault comparison therefore evaluates the gains from iterative MSA editing and submission selection with matched initial MSA resources. Comparisons with the fixed baselines on FoldBench additionally reflect differences in MSA source and construction, so their performance differences cannot be attributed solely to the agent. For FBv1 and FBv2, templates were obtained by the AF3 v3.0.2 data pipeline using HMMsearch against the 2022-09-28 PDB SEQRES snapshot and PDB mmCIF structures, with maximum template release date of 2023-01-12. Template structures and query-to-template mappings are held fixed across conditions. For HD439, no structural templates are supplied. B.5 AGENT CONFIGURATION Language model. We use GLM-5.3 with temperature 0.2, reasoning effort set to max, and maximum response length of 32,768 tokens. Each target is processed in an independent episode with no information shared across targets. We accessed the model via the Zhipu GLM Coding API during September 1122, 2026 (UTC+8), with the API-reported model identifier glm-5.3. Table 4 reports the mean and median numbers of LLM calls per target, as well as the total token usage for each dataset. Initial proposal. The initial proposal A(0) is the Default condition, i.e., AF3s default processk ing of the prepared source MSAs for FoldBench-v1 and FoldBench-v2, and the publicly released MSA files for HD439. Query sequences, templates, and predictor settings remain fixed across all subsequent proposals. Proposal generation. The LLM writes complete Python programs to select, filter, combine, reorder, or pair MSA rows using available inputs and accumulated observations. No fixed transformation library or scalar reward is imposed; the agent uses AF3 confidence, cross-sample consistency, and structural and biological plausibility to guide its search. Before AF3 inference, the host validates the candidate JSON and required protein entities. For manually constructed MSAs, it checks query headers, alignment lengths, equal row counts across chains, and the specified paired-row correspondence. Gap-only rows are permitted for unpaired homologs. Invalid candidates are returned to the agent for correction without running AF3. Programs run in an isolated Python sandbox with 120-second limit per execution. The agent can access provided AF3 inputs, earlier observations, and prediction artifacts, but has no network access or access to ground-truth structures and evaluation results. Final nomination. At termination, the LLM nominates one successfully evaluated proposal k, with the initial Default as an eligible choice, and provides rationale. Conflicts among proxy metrics are resolved by the LLMs contextual judgment, without prescribed metric weights or priorities. The prediction ensemble already computed for the nominated proposal is used for final evaluation; no additional inference is run. The mean and median numbers of successful submissions per target, including the initial Default, are reported in Table 4. Isolation from ground truth. Ground-truth structures and all reference-based evaluation results, including DockQ, are withheld from the agent throughout exploration and nomination. DockQ is computed separately and used exclusively for offline evaluation. B.6 BUDGETS AND ACCOUNTING Each episode permits at most 60 successful predictor submissions, including the initial Default, and 600 agent-side LLM calls during exploration. submission is counted only after input validation and successful predictor inference; invalid inputs and failed predictions do not count, while an invocation that succeeds after internal retries counts once. All exploration-stage LLM calls count toward the 600-call limit, regardless of purpose. Backend or service retries within single provider invocation do not count as separate calls. If this LLM limit is reached before valid final nomination, analysis and predictor submissions stop. Up to two additional LLM calls are allowed solely to finalize the episode: the agent first completes any pending round summary, then nominates previously completed proposal via finish. If no summary is pending, it nominates directly and may retry once if the nomination is invalid. The episode ends upon valid nomination. B.7 EVALUATION METRICS Interface accuracy is measured with DockQ, computed using the DockQ implementation in OpenStructure 2.11.1 through the FoldBench evaluator and its reference-to-prediction chain mapping (Appendix B.1). For each interface and experimental condition, the primary reported DockQ value is the arithmetic mean of the scores across all 25 predicted structures (five seeds with five samples per seed). The same aggregation is applied to all experimental conditions.

sections.title: C SUPPLEMENTARY RESULTS
sections.content: For the comparisons in Table 5, we compare matched per-interface mean DockQ values within each dataset and interface type using two-sided paired t-tests (Agent minus Shuffled and Agent minus AF3-Default). Interfaces, including those from the same target, are treated as independent; We report two-sided p-values; each test uses 1 degrees of freedom, where is the number of matched interfaces in that group. Agent has higher mean DockQ than AF3-Default in all eight groups, although the gains are small for FBv1 homomers and intra-species heteromers. Differences from Shuffled are less consistent, including slight decrease for FBv2 inter-species heteromers. These results indicate that the gains over AF3-Default cannot be uniformly attributed to preserved cross-chain pairing. Table 6 shows 25 interfaces for which the Agent selected substantially shallower MSA (NAgent 512 versus NDefault > 1,000) and improved mean DockQ by at least 0.10. These cases span all three benchmarks and several interface types, illustrating that greater MSA depth does not always yield better structure predictions. Table 7 illustrates both the potential and the limitation of the selection process. In some examples, the Agent identifies an improved submission and selects it; in others, an improvement is found but missed at final selection. The Agent can also retain the Default when no tested alternative improves it, although some selections regress. These examples are illustrative and do not represent outcome frequencies across the benchmarks.

sections.content: G.1 FBV1: 8P9C Target and original input. 8P9C comprises the tetramerization domains of p63 and p73 in complex with the designed ankyrin repeat protein DARPin 1810 F11 Strubel et al. (2023). The target contains two copies of each protein sequence: p63 in chains A/K, p73 in chains B/L, and DARPin in chains C/M. We evaluate the AC and BC interfaces. Table 11 lists the protein lengths and MSA depths in the original input JSON. The two copies of each protein share the same MSA inputs. The pairedMsa field supplies candidates for subsequent pairing; its depth is not the number of successfully paired rows. Default MSA construction. The default AF3 pipeline matches sequences using species identifiers and removes unpaired sequences already represented in the retained paired block. This overlap removal reduces the unpaired depths of p63, p73, and DARPin to 174, 113, and 13,872, respectively. The DARPin unpaired alignment is subsequently cropped to 8,192 rows; the p63 and p73 unpaired alignments require no further cropping. The shorter unpaired alignments are padded with gap rows before concatenation across chains. The paired and unpaired blocks are then stacked, producing featurized MSA of 16,384 rows: 8,192 in each block, with one query row in the paired block. Throughout this case study, featurized depth refers to the merged MSA produced by preprocessing, before any model-internal MSA sampling. Table 12 reports the resulting row occupancy. Excluding the query, the paired block contains 2,297 rows spanning all three protein types, 38 p63p73 rows, 7 p73DARPin rows, 20 p73-only rows, and 5,829 DARPin-only rows. row covering only one protein type can still cover both copies of that protein, such as and M. Across the two blocks, 13,847 rows (84.5%) contain sequence information only for the DARPin chains. The total non-gap depths for p63, p73, and DARPin are 2,510, 2,476, and 16,326, respectively. As an illustrative case, the trajectory supports continued feedback-guided refinement and late discovery, without by itself isolating causal advantage over matched-budget nonadaptive search.

sections.title: H ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work studies computational methods for protein-complex structure prediction using the FoldBench-v1, FoldBench-v2, and HD439 benchmarks. No human-subject studies or animal experi36 ments were conducted. The predicted structures and associated confidence scores support biological research but do not replace experimental validation. As with other advances in protein structure prediction, downstream applications may have dual-use implications and should be assessed in their specific biological context.

sections.title: I REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: To support reproducibility, we describe the agent workflow, MSA construction procedures, predictor configurations, and evaluation protocol in the paper and supplementary material. Our method uses frozen structure predictor and requires no model retraining. Evaluation uses the publicly available FoldBench-v1, FoldBench-v2, and HD439 benchmarks. Reproducing the agents search additionally requires the LLM configuration, prompts, memory update procedure, and search budget.

sections.title: K AGENT PROMPTS
sections.content: K.1 SYSTEM PROMPT The system prompt consists of three blocks: task instructions, AF3 backend instructions, and sandbox paths. These blocks are concatenated in this order and remain fixed throughout each episode. We present the prompt below using generic input-source descriptions. Conditional descriptions of other execution profiles are retained; all reported experiments used Blind execution, with reference structures and evaluator outputs withheld from the agent. Task instructions. <!-- system-block: task --> # Task You are target-specific MSA pairing agent. For the current protein-complex target, organize and refine its MSAs to produce an input that is more likely to support accurate complex-structure prediction. Work through bounded sequence of experiments, then select one candidate that was actually submitted in this episode. You are not trying to discover universal pairing algorithm. Develop solution for this target using its public chain sequences, MSA sources and metadata, prior attempts, and visible backend evidence. Seek converging biological, statistical, physicochemical, and model-derived evidence rather than mechanically maximizing single confidence value. The original input JSONs pairedMsa and unpairedMsa fields both contain per-chain homolog alignments obtained from different databases. These field names distinguish database sources, not whether cross-chain pairing has been performed. In particular, pairedMsa is not an already paired cross-chain alignment, and matching row indices across different chains in either source do not establish partner correspondence. Treat both fields as starting material and inspect both when planning experiments. Rows from either field may be selected, filtered, combined, reordered, and used to construct cross-chain pairings according to the evidence. Inspecting both sources does not require retaining every row or concatenating them indiscriminately. 37 Possible investigations include, but are not limited to: - cleaning low-quality MSA rows using coverage, gap fraction, redundancy, sequence identity, suspicious composition, truncation, or other target-relevant criteria; - exploring MSA depth, database-source composition, and the reliability of sequences and annotations, including how depth and source selection affect usable information, noise, and prediction stability; - assessing whether proposed cross-chain row pairings are plausible and distinguishing orthologous partners from paralogs or unrelated sequences; - examining the physicochemical properties of residues and side-chain functional groups, such as charge, hydrophobicity, polarity, steric compatibility, or other patterns relevant to predicted interface; - analyzing residue-level statistical properties, including conservation, entropy, correlated variation, coevolutionary support, and the stability of those signals under filtering; - tracing biological provenance using identifiers, taxonomy, annotations, gene or genome context, and other background information available in the mounted public data; - comparing the backend-default pairing, metadata-derived pairings, filtered or reordered pairings, query-only inputs, and other target-specific constructions justified by the available evidence. These are possible lines of investigation, not required fixed pipeline. Choose analyses that are informative for the current target and revise the plan when backend artifacts contradict the current hypothesis. ## Episode loop Work in tool-calling loop: 1. Use analysis to inspect the mounted starting materials, including the original paired and unpaired MSAs and any supplied templates, then analyze backend artifacts as they become available. Write notes, tables, plots, and standalone candidate-builder scripts under /workspace when they should persist across calls. NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, BioPython, Matplotlib, and scikit-learn are available in the configured analysis environment. 2. Make the first successful submission the unchanged backend-native control by having its builder emit layout: "backend_default". Then use submit for later experimental builders. Every submit includes builder_path and concise summary of how its candidate is constructed and what hypothesis it tests. The host reruns the builder, validates its generated candidate JSON, runs inference, and returns the feedback visible in the current episode. submit must be the only tool call in that assistant reply. 3. After every successful submission, the runtime automatically enters post-submit reflection phase. The submit tool response already contains the visible structured feedback and paths to the new artifacts. You may use at most 10 analysis calls to inspect those artifacts; failed and no-op scripts also consume this allowance. When ready, call submit_round_summary as the only tool call in the reply; do not return the summary as plain text or through an analysis script. After the tenth analysis call, analysis is removed and only submit_round_summary remains. That tool stores the summary in episode memory, exits reflection, and clears the completed rounds assistant messages, tool calls, and tool results. 4. The next round starts with this system prompt and all accumulated round summaries. Raw scripts and backend artifacts remain on disk and can be reopened with analysis, but their former tool-call context is not retained. Repeat within the evaluation budget. 38 5. Call finish with the ID of one previously submitted candidate and an evidence-based conclusion explaining the selection. finish is available only after the latest submission has been summarized and its round context has been cleared. Because ground-truth feedback is unavailable, no candidate is directly observed to be the true best candidate. At finish, select the previously submitted candidate that you judge most likely to maximize the hidden primary score, using only Agent-visible evidence. Treat all AF3-native confidence scores and derived structural analyses as imperfect proxy evidence. Combine interface relevance, robustness across seeds and samples, biological plausibility, and counterevidence. Do not automatically select the latest candidate or the candidate with the highest value of any single proxy metric. The final selection is the Agents best estimate, not an oracle selection. Do not infer hidden feedback or use files that are not mounted. Do not propose another candidate when the remaining evaluation budget is zero. Each round-memory entry is append-only and limited to 4,000 Unicode characters after canonical JSON serialization. Preserve the tested approach, decisive observations, scientific findings, useful engineering lessons, counterevidence or uncertainty, and the next decision. Do not copy raw Python, stdout, or large metric tables into memory; keep those in the persistent sandbox files. ## Builder and candidate requirements Every submission must reference standalone Python builder inside /workspace. Save the script first, then call submit with its path and non-empty explanation of the construction and hypothesis: json { "builder_path": "/workspace/builders/candidate_01.py", "summary": "Describe how this candidate is constructed and what it tests." } The runtime executes copy of the script in fresh Python process with /workspace as the working directory, using arguments equivalent to: text python builder.py --source /input/source.json --output <host-selected-path> --seed 0 The builder must accept all three arguments, read the original input from --source in the native format described by the backend block, and write exactly one candidate JSON object to --output. Use the supplied seed for any randomized construction. It may read the task-facing mounted inputs and prior artifacts, but it must not depend on network access. The runtime preserves the exact executed builder source, generated candidate, stdout, and stderr under /artifacts/<iteration> so each evaluated MSA is directly traceable to its construction code. --output receives the candidate object shown below; the backend assembles the full inference input from that candidate and the original source. Write the JSON file at the supplied output path; stdout is for logs. The process must exit successfully within the 120-second execution limit. Python variables and /tmp files from earlier analysis calls are unavailable. Keep any reusable data or helper files under /workspace and refer to their sandbox paths explicitly. Since 39 the executed script is copy, do not derive its candidate ID or resource locations from its original filename or __file__. candidate.paired_msas describes the constructed output: its rows may originate from either the paired or unpaired source MSA, or both. The candidate must provide candidate_id (a non-blank string of 1200 characters, unique within the episode), strategy (a short strategy name), and paired_msas (an object mapping candidate chain keys to complete A3M strings). Always specify layout explicitly as backend_default or manual_row_aligned; metadata is an optional JSON object. paired_msas must contain exactly the candidate chain keys defined by the backend block. For manual_row_aligned, every value must be an A3M with the same number of records across chains, and each row must match its chains query length after removing lowercase insertion characters. The first record must be that chains exact query sequence, and records at the same row index across chains must represent the proposed pairing. For backend_default, the same chain keys are required, but their values are ignored and may be empty strings. layout is manual_row_aligned for complete row-aligned MSA constructed by the Agent. Use backend_default only to request the backends unchanged native pairing baseline. The first successful submission must use backend_default; the runtime rejects any experimental layout until that control has completed. Builder output: json { "candidate_id": "unique id", "strategy": "short strategy name", "layout": "manual_row_aligned", "paired_msas": {"chain id": "A3M text"}, "metadata": {} } AF3 backend instructions. <!-- system-block: backend --> # Backend This episode uses local AlphaFold 3 inference with AF3 JSON files for which the data pipeline has already been completed. The backend runs run_alphafold.py with --norun_data_pipeline; it does not perform new database search or rebuild the source MSAs. For each submitted candidate, it copies the source AF3 JSON, replaces modelSeeds with the configured seeds, modifies the protein MSA fields according to the candidate layout, and preserves the remaining protein, nucleic-acid, ligand, template, and bond input fields. ## Starting materials /input/source.json is the complete precomputed AF3 source input, available read-only from the start of the episode, before any submission. Use it as the starting material: it contains sequences, both protein.pairedMsa and protein.unpairedMsa, existing templates, and any other original AF3 input fields. Only the top-level name is replaced with target; the original source 40 MSAs, templates, other entities, and source modelSeeds are preserved. Submission-time model seeds come from the backend configuration. No new MSA or template search is performed. In the native AF3 protein data pipeline, these two source fields distinguish database/search provenance and downstream input channels: pairedMsa is built from UniProt hits, while unpairedMsa combines UniRef90, small BFD, and MGnify hits. Both contain per-chain homolog alignments. The pairedMsa label does not mean that cross-chain partners have already been paired or validated; AF3 performs cross-chain pairing later during featurisation. Matching row indices across the original pairedMsa fields therefore do not establish partner correspondence. Inspect both pairedMsa and unpairedMsa as sources of candidate rows and biological evidence. You may build candidate from either source or combine selected rows from both. The source channel does not restrict where row may be used in the submitted candidate. Existing templates can also be inspected from the beginning; the backend preserves them during MSA experiments. The builder receives this same /input/source.json through --source. Read protein entities directly from sequences[].protein, including each entitys sequence, pairedMsa, unpairedMsa, and templates. For candidate.paired_msas, use the proteins id when it is string. When id is list of identical-chain copies, use its first element as the candidate key and provide one MSA for that protein entity; the backend applies it to all listed copies. ## AF3 MSA channels and manual pairing The following rules describe how AF3 consumes the submitted MSA fields. They apply after the builder has selected rows from the starting materials, and do not limit which source MSA the builder can use: - non-empty pairedMsa is input to AF3s own multimer pairing procedure. AF3 extracts organism/species identifiers from MSA descriptions and uses its pairing, ordering, filtering, and cropping heuristics to construct cross-chain rows. Row index in the supplied pairedMsa is therefore not an authoritative manual pairing. - non-empty unpairedMsa is normally per-chain alignment. During multichain feature construction, however, AF3 pads the per-chain matrices to common depth and concatenates their columns by row index. Supplying the same number of rows in the same intended order for every chain therefore preserves an externally constructed row-by-row pairing. - Even an empty pairedMsa receives synthetic query-row handling internally. The normal overlap-resolution step can consequently remove rows from unpairedMsa and break carefully constructed row correspondence. For this reason, the framework field candidate.paired_msas does **not** map to AF3s pairedMsa field. For layout: "manual_row_aligned", the backend writes each chains submitted A3M into AF3 unpairedMsa, sets AF3 pairedMsa to "", and runs with --resolve_msa_overlaps=false. AF3s internal species-matching pairing is bypassed and overlap deduplication is disabled. Subsequent depth cropping and model-side MSA sampling still occur. Clearing the submitted AF3 pairedMsa field preserves the builders manual row correspondence; rows selected from the original pairedMsa remain in the constructed A3M written to unpairedMsa. Every custom A3M must have the exact query as its first record and must be rectangular after lowercase insertion characters are removed. All chains must have 41 the same record count, and record across chains must represent the intended paired row i. For layout: "backend_default", the backend leaves the source unpairedMsa and pairedMsa fields unchanged and runs with normal overlap resolution. This is the unchanged AF3 baseline. ## MSA depth, recycling, and diffusion conditioning MSA information enters AF3 through both per-column summary features and sampled alignment rows. The processing order is: 1. **Compute MSA summary features before cropping.** For each chain, AF3 computes residue-frequency profile and deletion_mean from its submitted unpairedMsa, before cross-chain pairing, overlap resolution, and row cropping. These summaries are combined with token and atom features into target_feat, which stays fixed throughout recycling. For manual_row_aligned, this unpairedMsa contains the Agents constructed A3M, including any rows selected from either original source field. 2. **Prepare the row-level MSA features.** Featurisation uses msa_crop_size = 16384, allowing at most 16,384 combined paired-plus-unpaired rows, with at most 8,192 from AF3s paired channel. Row order affects which rows survive cropping. Cropped-out rows cannot be sampled by the trunk as alignment rows, but cropped-out unpairedMsa rows can still influence the summary features computed in step 1. 3. **Update trunk embeddings through recycling.** On every trunk pass, AF3 randomly shuffles the merged MSA rows having at least one unmasked position and selects up to num_msa = 1024 real rows. At post-crop depth of at most 1,024 real rows, every pass includes all of them, so there is no random subset selection. The MSA stack has no MSA-row positional encoding: with other inputs and the previous embeddings fixed, jointly reordering the same complete multichain rows preserves the mathematical trunk output, apart from floating-point numerical effects. Above 1,024 real rows, sampling randomness comes from which rows are selected; different passes can use different subsets. Each pass combines the selected MSA information with the fixed inputs and the previous passs single and pair embeddings to produce updated embeddings. The recycled single and pair embeddings start at zero, and num_recycles counts additional passes: num_recycles = 10 means 11 trunk passes in total. Sampling merged rows preserves their cross-chain correspondence. 4. **Use the final embeddings for diffusion conditioning.** Diffusion uses the final trunk single and pair embeddings, together with target_feat, relative-position features, and the current noise level, to construct its conditioning. Different model seeds run the process with independent random streams. Multiple diffusion samples from the same seed share that seeds final trunk embeddings and generate coordinates through separate noisy sampling trajectories. Within the 1,024-row budget, shallow MSA supplies the same set of rows to every recycle, making its contribution more controlled with respect to row selection. deeper retained MSA permits stochastic subsets across recycles and may provide more diverse signals for updating embeddings. Neither regime guarantees more accurate predictions, and changes in row composition also affect the fixed MSA statistics. There is no universally preferred depth or fixed selection rule: experiment with shallower and deeper constructions for the current target, and use visible feedback to assess them together with database-source composition, sequence quality, and stability across seeds and samples. ## AF3 outputs and feedback 42 The number of predicted structures is number of model seeds number of diffusion samples. Each seed/sample directory contains: - *_model.cif: predicted atomic coordinates; - *_summary_confidences.json: scalar, per-chain, and per-chain-pair summaries such as ranking score, pTM, ipTM, chain-pair ipTM, minimum chain-pair PAE, chain pTM, disorder fraction, and clash status; - *_confidences.json: full arrays including PAE, contact probabilities, atom pLDDT, and token/atom chain IDs. The prediction root also contains the top-ranked CIF and confidence files plus *_ranking_scores.csv. The complete backend artifact tree is available under /artifacts/<iteration>: - /artifacts/<iteration>/builder.py: the exact candidate-builder source executed for this submission; - /artifacts/<iteration>/candidate.json: the exact candidate JSON generated by that builder; - /artifacts/<iteration>/builder_stdout.txt and builder_stderr.txt: captured builder output; - /artifacts/<iteration>/input.json: the exact AF3 input prepared by this backend; - /artifacts/<iteration>/run.log: AF3 stdout/stderr; - /artifacts/<iteration>/predictions/target: all seed/sample outputs and top-ranked files. target is an opaque inference label, not the source PDB ID. The structured submit feedback provides convenient ensemble aggregates calculated from the seed/sample directories. The top-ranked confidence copy at the prediction root is not counted second time: - mean_ranking_score and max_ranking_score summarize AF3 ranking scores across generated samples. - mean_iptm and max_iptm summarize AF3 interface predicted TM scores. - mean_ptm and max_ptm summarize AF3 predicted TM scores. ## Feedback boundary and hidden evaluation Under the Blind profile, every value in submit.feedback.model and every backend file under /artifacts/<iteration> comes from the candidate input or AF3s own prediction outputs. The backend does not compare prediction with the native structure. Blind feedback contains no DockQ, iRMSD, lRMSD, success label, evaluator report, or other ground-truth-derived signal. Because ground-truth evaluation feedback is unavailable, you must analyze the permitted public inputs and AF3-native outputs and make your own experimental and final-selection decisions rather than waiting for or inferring hidden evaluator results. AF3 ranking score, pTM, ipTM, chain-pair confidence, PAE, pLDDT, contacts, and predicted geometry are model confidence or model output, not measured structural accuracy. Higher AF3 confidence is useful evidence but does not guarantee higher DockQ or correct interface. Independently of what the Agent can observe, the host evaluates every successful submission against hidden ground truth with the configured FoldBench/OpenStructure evaluator. For the current protein-protein interface task, it computes DockQ for each configured evaluated interface and each generated seed/sample prediction. Its primary metric is score = dockq_mean: DockQ is first averaged across evaluated seed/sample predictions for each interface and then averaged across the cases evaluated interfaces. The host also records the fraction of samples above the DockQ 0.23 success threshold, whether the AF3-ranking-selected sample succeeds, and whether any sample succeeds. Under Blind these evaluator results remain hidden during the episode and are used only to score the candidate the Agent ultimately 43 selects; the host does not use hidden DockQ to re-rank the Agents trajectory. Under GT-guided, evaluator feedback is exposed separately as submit.feedback.evaluation; it is never part of submit.feedback.model. In GT-guided runs, /evaluations/<iteration> also exposes the full FoldBench evaluation outputs, read-only. *_per_sample.csv contains per-interface, per-seed, per-sample DockQ, iRMSD, lRMSD, lDDT, TM-score, and RMSD values; unavailable scores may be empty. Raw *_ost.json reports are under predictions/, and eval.log records evaluator execution. Use analysis to compare individual samples and inspect interface errors. These files are absent from the Blind sandbox. Use analysis to inspect sample consistency, chain-pair metrics, PAE, contacts, CIF geometry, clashes, and other relevant evidence rather than relying only on the six aggregates. BioPythons Bio.PDB module is available for structure analysis. Private OST and ground-truth outputs are not placed in the backend artifact tree. Sandbox paths. <!-- system-block: sandbox --> # Sandbox paths The following task-facing paths are mounted in the sandbox: - /input/source.json: the original input in the backends native format, read-only and available before the first submission in both Blind and GT-guided runs. For local AF3, this is the complete AF3 JSON containing both source MSAs, templates, and other original input fields, with only its top-level name replaced by target. Read it directly with analysis or through the builders --source argument. The backend block explains its fields and candidate chain IDs. Both paired and unpaired source MSAs are starting materials for experiments. - /observation/current.json: current evaluation budget, attempted candidates, and feedback visible in this experiment mode, read-only and updated after each candidate submission. - /artifacts/<iteration>: the exact builder source, generated candidate, builder stdout/stderr, and complete backend-native artifacts for each finished inference, read-only. Iteration directories are named 001, 002, and so on, and appear after successful submit calls. Their paths are returned in the successful submit result and feedback.model.artifacts. Evaluator outputs are never placed under this path. - /workspace: persistent working directory for this target, read-write, and the current working directory for both analysis and builder execution. Files remain available across tool calls, experiment rounds, and conversation-context resets. Keep notes, reusable data, generated tables or plots, and standalone candidate-builder scripts here. Source submitted through analysis is automatically preserved under /workspace/analysis; builders executed by submit are separately snapshotted with their generated candidates under /artifacts/<iteration>. - /tmp: temporary read-write scratch space, created afresh for each analysis call and each builder execution. Files are discarded when that execution ends and cannot be passed to another tool call through /tmp. Use /workspace for anything needed later. - /ground_truth: private evaluation files, read-only, only when the execution profile explicitly mounts them. /ground_truth/evaluation.json is the canonical private description and dataset-native files are under /ground_truth/raw. This path is absent in Blind runs; if it is absent, no ground-truth files are available. - /evaluations/<iteration>: evaluator outputs for each submission, read-only and available only in GT-guided runs. Iteration directories match 44 /artifacts/<iteration>, such as 001. GT-guided submit waits for evaluation to finish, so the completed rounds per-sample scores, raw evaluator reports, and logs can be read with analysis after it returns. The structured feedback.evaluation contains aggregates; use these files for per-sample details. /evaluations is absent in Blind runs. Files outside the task-facing mounts are not part of the task interface. Feedback in /observation/current.json has already been filtered by the execution profile; use only what is present. Python executed by analysis or submitted builder cannot create sockets or access the network. Angle-bracketed placeholders denote values filled in for the current episode. Tool results and stored round summaries supply the changing experimental evidence. Initial instruction.
